title: Tissues
tagline: Plant and animal tissues: what they are made of, where each one sits, and the job each performs.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every tissue location and function below is standard histology. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A tissue is a group of cells that are similar in structure and work together to perform one particular function, so tissues are the level of organisation between the cell and the organ. This chapter works through plant tissues first, dividing them into meristematic tissues that keep dividing and permanent tissues that have taken on a fixed role, then the simple and complex permanent tissues. It then turns to the four animal tissues — epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous — and treats each type as a structure designed for a job, because in animal histology the location of a tissue tells you almost everything about its shape.

facts.label: Definition
facts.value: A group of similar cells performing a common function

facts.label: Fastest-dividing plant tissue
facts.value: Apical meristem at the tip of root and shoot

learningOutcomes: Define tissue and explain why cells organise into tissues.
Classify plant tissues into meristematic and permanent, and permanent tissues into simple and complex.
Relate the structure of each animal tissue type to its function and give its location in the body.
Compare tissues that are commonly confused, such as tendon against ligament and striated against cardiac muscle.

blocks.text: Plant tissues are divided first by whether the cells still divide. Meristematic tissues consist of thin-walled, densely packed cells with large nuclei and little vacuolation, and they divide actively throughout the plant's life. Apical meristem at the tips of roots and shoots increases the length of the plant, lateral meristem or cambium increases its girth by producing wood, and intercalary meristem at the base of leaves and internodes allows a grass to keep growing after it has been grazed. Because division demands energy, meristematic cells are metabolically very active and store little food. Once a cell stops dividing it enlarges and differentiates into a permanent tissue, which may be simple — one kind of cell — or complex, containing several kinds of cell working as a conducting system.

items: Meristematic cells are thin-walled because a thick wall would resist the repeated division that is their whole purpose.
Permanent tissues are of two kinds: simple (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) and complex (xylem and phloem).
Parenchyma that contains chloroplasts is called chlorenchyma and carries out photosynthesis.
Collenchyma gives flexibility to a young stem so it can bend in wind without snapping.
Sclerenchyma cells are dead at maturity and heavily lignified, which is why a coconut husk is so tough.
The epidermis of a desert leaf may bear a thick cuticle and sunken stomata to conserve water.
Stomatal opening and closing is controlled by the guard cells, which change shape as they take in water.

items.text: The husk of a coconut is sclerenchyma: dead, lignified cells packed so tightly that the shell resists a blow and protects the seed inside.
items.note: Use a familiar object to anchor the fact that sclerenchyma is dead at maturity.

items.text: The thin, flexible green stem of a young plant owes its ability to bend without breaking to collenchyma just below the epidermis; by the time the stem becomes woody, sclerenchyma and lignified xylem have taken over that support.
items.note: The same organ is supported by different tissues at different stages of growth.

blocks.text: Epithelial tissue covers every surface of the body — outside the skin, inside the gut, and lining the ducts and cavities — and it is always a closely packed sheet of cells sitting on a basement membrane with no blood supply of its own. Its shape and layering follow the abuse it must take. Squamous epithelium is a single layer of flat cells, thin enough to allow diffusion, and lines the alveoli of the lungs and the capillary walls. Cuboidal epithelium forms kidneys and gland ducts. Columnar epithelium lines the intestine and often bears cilia on its free surface. Where wear is heavy, several layers pile up into stratified squamous epithelium, as in the skin and oesophagus. Glandular epithelium is columnar or cuboidal cells modified to secrete, and may be a single-celled gland or a multicellular gland such as the salivary gland.

Connective tissue is the most widely distributed tissue of the body and, unlike epithelium, it has a great deal of intercellular matrix whose nature decides the tissue's properties. In areolar tissue the matrix is a soft gel holding collagen and elastin fibres, and it packs organs together, fills spaces and supports blood vessels. Adipose tissue stores fat as an insulating and energy-reserving layer beneath the skin. In bone the matrix is hard and mineralised with calcium salts, so it gives a rigid skeleton and protects the brain, spinal cord and lungs. Cartilage has a firm but flexible matrix of chondrin and is found at joint surfaces, the tracheal rings and the external ear. Blood is a fluid connective tissue in which the matrix is plasma, and it carries oxygen, nutrients, wastes and heat. Tendons join muscle to bone and are tough inelastic cords, while ligaments join bone to bone and are elastic.

items.meaning: The thin layer of matrix on which an epithelial sheet sits; it is not a blood supply, which epithelia lack.
The non-cellular material between the cells of a connective tissue; its consistency determines the tissue's properties.
Arranged in several layers, as stratified squamous epithelium, which resists abrasion.
Connective tissue specialised for storing fat, forming an insulating subcutaneous layer.
Hair-like projections of a cell surface whose beating moves material along, as in the trachea.

items.text: The lining of the alveoli is one cell thick so that oxygen and carbon dioxide can cross quickly, while the skin is many cells thick so that nothing can easily get through.
items.note: Both are squamous epithelium — the layer count is what changes.

items.text: A joint such as the knee has cartilage covering the bone ends to reduce friction, a capsule of ligament holding the bones together, and a tendon attaching the thigh muscle to the shin bone.
items.note: One joint illustrates four connective tissues at once.

blocks.text: Muscular tissue is built from elongated cells called muscle fibres that contract using a protein mechanism, and it exists in three forms with different structures and levels of control. Striated or skeletal muscle has fibres marked by light and dark bands, is attached to the skeleton, and is under voluntary control, so you can decide to lift an arm. Smooth muscle has spindle-shaped fibres with no banding, lines hollow organs such as the stomach, intestine and blood vessels, contracts slowly and rhythmically, and is involuntary. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart wall; its fibres are branched, joined at intercalated discs, striated like skeletal muscle but involuntary like smooth muscle, and it contracts rhythmically without fatigue throughout life. Nervous tissue, the fourth animal tissue, consists of neurons supported by neuroglia. A neuron has a cell body with a nucleus, short branching dendrites that carry impulses towards the cell body, and one long axon that carries the impulse away, often wrapped in a fatty myelin sheath that speeds conduction.

blocks.caption: The three kinds of muscle compared
rows: Spindle shaped, pointed at both ends
Short, branched, joined at intercalated discs
Walls of stomach, intestine, uterus, blood vessels

items: Striated muscle is voluntary because its contraction is triggered by a nerve impulse you consciously initiate.
Smooth muscle contracts without conscious control, which is why digestion proceeds while you sleep.
Cardiac muscle is branched and joined by intercalated discs so that the whole heart wall contracts as one coordinated wave.
The three muscle types share the same basic sliding-filament mechanism of contraction; they differ in control and arrangement.
A neuron's axon can be very long — the axon reaching from the spine to the foot is over a metre in length.
Myelin is an electrical insulator, so a myelinated axon conducts a nerve impulse far faster than a bare one.
Neuroglia are support cells that nourish, protect and repair neurons; they are far more numerous than neurons.
Dendrites carry the impulse towards the cell body and the axon carries it away — a distinction examiners check directly.

items.text: You can deliberately stop lifting a book, but you cannot deliberately stop your stomach from churning: skeletal muscle is voluntary and smooth muscle is involuntary.
items.note: Contrast two actions you can feel to make the control distinction concrete.

items.text: The wall of the heart keeps beating in rhythm because cardiac fibres are linked at intercalated discs that let the excitation spread from fibre to fibre without any nerve input.
items.note: This also explains why the heart can beat when removed from the body under the right conditions.

learn.title: Putting tissues together: comparison and application

blocks.text: Much of the marks in a tissue question come from distinguishing pairs that are easy to swap: tendon against ligament, epithelial against connective, striated against cardiac muscle, and xylem against phloem. The reliable way to answer is to start from function and let structure follow. A tendon must transmit a powerful pull in one direction only, so it is a cord of dense parallel collagen fibres with almost no elasticity; a ligament must hold two bones at a joint while still allowing movement, so it is elastic and runs bone to bone. Epithelium covers and lines surfaces, is avascular and regenerates rapidly; connective tissue is everywhere, is supplied with blood, and its matrix does the work. Recognising a tissue from a micrograph or a description is the same reasoning in reverse: look at the cell shape, the amount of matrix, and whether the tissue is banding-free or banded, then place it.

items: Tendon = muscle to bone, inelastic, parallel fibres; ligament = bone to bone, elastic, holds joints together.
Epithelial tissue is avascular and sits on a basement membrane; connective tissue is vascular and has abundant matrix.
Xylem carries water and minerals upward only and is dead at maturity; phloem carries dissolved food both ways and its sieve tubes are living.
Cartilage is avascular, which is why it heals slowly — a fact worth knowing when a joint injury is discussed.
Blood is classed as connective tissue because its cells lie in a fluid matrix called plasma.
A tissue section with a single layer of flat cells lining a space is squamous epithelium; one with heavy intercellular matrix is connective.
When asked to identify a tissue from a description, quote the shape of the cells and the amount of matrix before naming it.
Smooth muscle is involuntary and non-striated; cardiac muscle is involuntary and striated; striated muscle is voluntary.

items.text: The wall of a blood vessel is lined by thin squamous endothelium for a smooth, leak-resistant surface, surrounded by smooth muscle that alters the vessel diameter, and wrapped in areolar tissue that anchors it.
items.note: One vessel, three tissue types — a compact way to show how tissues combine into an organ.

items.text: A section through skin shows stratified squamous epithelium at the surface for protection, areolar dermis beneath carrying vessels and nerves, adipose tissue underneath for insulation, and smooth muscle attached to hair follicles.
items.note: Skin is the standard example of an organ built from several tissues.

figures.caption: Figure: Simple animal epithelia
figures.description: Four panels sharing a basement membrane drawn as a single line. Squamous: one row of flat cells with flat nuclei. Cuboidal: one row of cube-shaped cells with round central nuclei. Columnar: one row of tall cells with nuclei near the base, some bearing cilia as a fringe on the upper surface. Stratified squamous: several layers, the bottom row cuboidal and the top rows flattened and peeling.

figures.caption: Figure: A motor neuron
figures.description: A star-shaped cell body containing a nucleus, with many short branching dendrites radiating from it and one long axon leaving it. The axon is wrapped in a series of sausage-shaped myelin sheath segments separated by gaps, enclosed at the far end by a branched axon terminal. A Schwann cell nucleus is drawn on each sheath segment.

figures.caption: Figure: The three muscle types
figures.description: Three separate drawings at the same scale. Skeletal muscle: long parallel unbranched fibres with clear transverse bands and several nuclei pressed against the edge of each fibre. Smooth muscle: separate spindle-shaped cells each with one central nucleus and no banding. Cardiac muscle: branched fibres with banding, joined end to end by dark vertical intercalated discs, one nucleus per cell.

keyPoints: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together to perform a common function.
Meristematic tissues keep dividing; apical meristem adds length, lateral meristem adds girth, intercalary meristem elongates the internode.
Simple permanent tissues are parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma; complex permanent tissues are xylem and phloem.
Sclerenchyma is dead at maturity with lignified walls; parenchyma and collenchyma remain living.
Epithelial tissue covers and lines surfaces, sits on a basement membrane, and has no blood supply of its own.
Connective tissue is identified by its abundant intercellular matrix, which may be gel, hard mineral, flexible chondrin or fluid plasma.
Tendon joins muscle to bone and is inelastic; ligament joins bone to bone and is elastic.
The three muscles: striated is voluntary and striated, smooth is involuntary and non-striated, cardiac is involuntary, striated and branched with intercalated discs.
A neuron has dendrites carrying the impulse to the cell body and one axon carrying it away, commonly wrapped in myelin.
Blood is a fluid connective tissue whose matrix is plasma.
examFocus: 'Describe and state the function of' tissue questions need three parts: cell shape, location, and function — a function without a location rarely earns full marks.
The tendon and ligament pair is asked repeatedly; write muscle-to-bone against bone-to-bone in the first line of the answer.
Classifying plant tissues needs the full hierarchy: meristematic or permanent, then simple or complex, then the individual name — skipping the levels costs marks.
In identification questions, name the tissue first and then justify it from the observed cell shape and matrix before describing the function.

vocabulary.meaning: A group of similar cells performing a common function.
Plant tissue whose cells divide actively and produce growth.
Strengthened with lignin, as in sclerenchyma and xylem, making the wall rigid and impermeable.
Sheet-like tissue covering body surfaces and lining cavities, avascular and on a basement membrane.
Non-cellular material surrounding the cells of a connective tissue.
Specialised junction between cardiac muscle cells that lets the heart contract as a unit.
The single long process of a neuron that carries the nerve impulse away from the cell body.
Under conscious control / not under conscious control.

questions.prompt: Which plant tissue keeps a grass stem growing after the top has been eaten by grazing animals?
questions.explanation: The intercalary meristem lies at the base of the internodes, well below the growing tip, so its cells can still divide and elongate even after the tip of the grass has been removed by grazing. The apical meristem sits at the very tip and would have been eaten, and lateral meristem adds girth rather than length.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the apical meristem because it is the most familiar meristem; it is the one destroyed by grazing.

questions.prompt: The tissue that joins a muscle to a bone is a __________, while the tissue that joins one bone to another at a joint is a __________.
questions.explanation: A tendon is a tough cord of dense parallel collagen fibres running from muscle to bone so that it transmits the pull of contraction without stretching. A ligament joins bone to bone, contains more elastic fibres, and holds the joint together while still allowing movement.
questions.commonMistake: Swapping the two. Anchor them by sound: tendon is attached to the pulling muscle, ligament is the lace that laces bones together.

questions.prompt: A tissue has a single layer of flat, thin cells resting on a basement membrane. Which body structure is it most likely to line?
options: The outer surface of the skin
The shaft of a long bone
questions.explanation: A single flat layer of squamous epithelium offers the shortest diffusion path, exactly what the alveoli need for oxygen and carbon dioxide to pass into and out of the blood. The skin is stratified squamous, bone is connective tissue, and the trachea is lined by ciliated columnar epithelium.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the skin because it is the most obvious surface. Skin must resist abrasion, so it is many layers thick, not one.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between parenchyma and sclerenchyma on the grounds of cell wall, condition of the cells at maturity, and function.
questions.answer: Parenchyma has thin, flexible cellulose walls, its cells are alive at maturity, and it carries out storage, photosynthesis when it contains chloroplasts, and packing of the plant. Sclerenchyma has thick, lignified walls, its cells are dead at maturity, and it provides rigid mechanical support and protection, as in a coconut husk or a seed coat.
questions.explanation: Three contrasts are asked for, and each one must be answered on both sides. The wall thickness, the living or dead condition, and the resulting function are the three standard distinctions, and pairing them correctly shows that support in sclerenchyma is possible precisely because the cells are dead and heavily lignified.
questions.commonMistake: Saying sclerenchyma is dead without explaining that lignification, which makes the wall impermeable, is what kills the cell.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of striated muscle tissue and relate three of its structural features to its function.
questions.answer: Striated muscle consists of long, unbranched cylindrical fibres that run parallel to one another, each with several nuclei pressed against the periphery of the fibre and with regular light and dark bands across its length. The bands arise from the orderly arrangement of contractile proteins within the fibre. The great length of each fibre allows a large amount of shortening, so the muscle can produce a strong pull over a distance. The multiple nuclei support the high protein turnover needed by a fibre that contracts repeatedly and rapidly. The parallel arrangement transmits the force of contraction along one line of pull towards the tendon. Being under voluntary control, the tissue contracts only when a nerve impulse arrives from the central nervous system.
questions.explanation: Structure must be given first — parallel unbranched fibres, banding, multiple peripheral nuclei — and then at least three features must each be tied to a functional consequence. Length to pulling power, multiple nuclei to protein turnover, and parallel arrangement to a single line of pull are three defensible links.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the bands but never explaining them, or giving functions with no structural basis. The question explicitly asks for the relation between the two.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is correctly matched?
options: Blood — fluid connective tissue with plasma as matrix
Cartilage — hard mineralised matrix of calcium salts
Tendon — joins bone to bone at a joint
Chlorenchyma — dead supporting tissue of the leaf vein
questions.answer: Blood — fluid connective tissue with plasma as matrix
questions.explanation: Blood is a connective tissue whose cells are suspended in the fluid matrix plasma, which is why it is classed as connective at all. Cartilage has a firm but flexible chondrin matrix rather than a mineralised one, bone is the tissue with calcium salts, a tendon joins muscle to bone, and chlorenchyma is living parenchyma containing chloroplasts.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing the hard calcium matrix to cartilage. Hard mineralisation is osseous tissue, that is bone; cartilage stays flexible.

questions.prompt: A micrograph shows a tissue made of spindle-shaped cells with no visible banding, each with a single central nucleus, arranged in overlapping layers around a lumen. Identify the tissue, name the organ it is likely to be part of, state whether its action is voluntary or involuntary, and give one further example from elsewhere in the body.
questions.answer: The tissue is smooth muscle. The spindle shape, absence of striations and single central nucleus distinguish it from skeletal muscle, which is striated and multinucleate, and from cardiac muscle, which is branched and striated. Its arrangement around a lumen indicates a hollow organ, most likely the wall of the intestine, stomach, uterus or a blood vessel. Its action is involuntary, contracting rhythmically without conscious control, so that peristalsis continues without attention. A further example is the smooth muscle of the iris that alters the size of the pupil, or the smooth muscle in the wall of an artery that regulates the vessel's diameter.
questions.explanation: Three clues must be read in order: cell shape gives the tissue type, the lumen gives the organ type, and the banding pattern settles the muscle category. Stating voluntary or involuntary then follows from the tissue being smooth muscle, and the additional example must be another hollow or involuntary site rather than a limb muscle.
questions.commonMistake: Naming the tissue as striated muscle because the cell layers look banded. Smooth muscle has no bands, and misreading this single feature collapses the whole answer.

questions.prompt: Name the three types of meristematic tissue according to position, and state the growth each one is responsible for.
questions.answer: Apical meristem occurs at the tips of roots and shoots and increases the length of the plant. Lateral meristem occurs along the sides of stems and roots and increases their girth by producing secondary tissues. Intercalary meristem occurs at the base of internodes and leaves and is responsible for the elongation of the internode.
questions.explanation: The three meristems are classified by position, so each answer must pair the position with the direction of growth it produces: tip to length, side to girth, base of internode to internode elongation. Naming a meristem without its position and effect earns only part of the credit.
questions.commonMistake: Describing apical meristem as producing both length and girth. Girth is exclusively the lateral meristem's job.

questions.prompt: Connective tissue is identified by the presence of a large amount of intercellular __________. In bone this matrix is hard and mineralised with calcium salts, in cartilage it is firm and flexible, and in blood it is the fluid __________.
questions.explanation: The matrix is the defining feature of connective tissue, and its composition decides the tissue's properties: mineralised calcium salts make bone rigid, chondrin makes cartilage firm but resilient, and the liquid plasma of blood allows it to flow while carrying dissolved gases, nutrients and wastes.
questions.commonMistake: Writing 'collagen' for the first blank. Collagen is a fibre within the matrix, not the matrix itself.

questions.prompt: Which feature distinguishes cardiac muscle from both striated skeletal muscle and smooth muscle?
options: It is the only muscle that contracts voluntarily
It has branched fibres joined by intercalated discs
It is the only muscle lacking stripes under the microscope
It is attached to the skeleton by tendons
questions.answer: It has branched fibres joined by intercalated discs
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is uniquely branched, with fibres joined at intercalated discs that let excitation spread from cell to cell so the heart wall contracts as one unit. It is involuntary like smooth muscle, it is striated like skeletal muscle, and it is never attached to the skeleton — those options each describe one of the other two types or none at all.
questions.commonMistake: Picking the option about stripes. Cardiac muscle is striated; it is smooth muscle that lacks stripes.

questions.prompt: Explain why the epithelium lining the air sacs of the lung and the epithelium forming the outer layer of the skin are built so differently, even though both are epithelial tissue.
questions.answer: The two sites impose opposite demands, and epithelium adapts its structure to the demand placed on it. The air sacs must let oxygen and carbon dioxide pass between air and blood with the least possible resistance, so their lining is a single thin layer of flat squamous cells only one cell thick, giving the shortest possible diffusion path. The outer skin is constantly scraped, bruised and attacked by microbes, so it needs a barrier rather than a pathway; it is therefore stratified squamous epithelium, many layers thick, with the surface cells dead and keratinised so that they can be shed and replaced without damage to the living layers beneath. Both are epithelial because both cover a surface and sit on a basement membrane, but layer count is traded against permeability.
questions.explanation: The answer must identify the opposing requirements — rapid diffusion against mechanical protection — and then show how layer count answers each one. Merely stating that one is squamous and the other stratified describes the difference without explaining it, which is the half of the question most often missed.
questions.commonMistake: Describing both tissues and never naming the demand that each meets, which leaves the explanation incomplete even when the facts are right.
